title: Faster Algorithms for Multimarginal Optimal Transport
authors: Brandon Augustino, Yue Sun, Atithi Acharya, Shouvanik Chakrabarti, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Shree Hari Sureshbabu, Charlie Che
abstract: We study algorithms for approximating the multimarginal optimal transport (MOT) distance, a generalization of the classic optimal transport distance, between $m$ discrete probability distributions each supported on at most $n$ points. We give a classical algorithm that computes a coupling between these marginals whose expected transportation cost is within an additive $\varepsilon > 0$ of the MOT distance in time $O(m^2 n^m \varepsilon^{-1}\mathrm{polylog}(m,n,\varepsilon^{-1}))$. This is, to our knowledge, the first bound for general MOT problems with simultaneous linear dependence on the dimension $n^m$ and on the accuracy parameter $\varepsilon^{-1}$, improving the prior state of the art.   On the quantum side, we give two algorithms that achieve speedups in dimension, though with worse accuracy dependence than classical approaches. First, we construct a quantum projected subgradient method for estimating the MOT distance within an additive $\varepsilon >0$ with runtime $O( m^3 n^{\frac{m}{2}+1} \varepsilon^{-2} \mathrm{polylog}(m,n,\varepsilon^{-1}))$. This algorithm works with the linear programming dual of the MOT problem, and does not return a coupling. We also give a quantum multimarginal Sinkhorn algorithm for entropy-regularized MOT. This algorithm returns an implicit description of an approximately optimal coupling with runtime $O(m^8n^{\frac{m+1}{2}} \varepsilon^{-5} \mathrm{polylog}(m,n,\varepsilon^{-1})))$ after the usual reduction from entropic MOT to unregularized MOT. We also record query lower bounds: for any precision $\varepsilon<1/2$, randomized classical algorithms require $Ω(n^m/(1+\varepsilon n))$ queries and quantum algorithms require $Ω(\sqrt{n^m/(1+\varepsilon n)})$ queries.
summary: This paper tackles the computational challenge of approximating multimarginal optimal transport (MOT) distance between multiple probability distributions using advanced algorithms. It provides both classical and quantum solutions, achieving specific runtime bounds for different formulations (primal vs. dual). The work is significant for establishing theoretical speedups in solving complex multi-marginal optimization problems.
main_problem: The core problem is developing efficient algorithms, both classical and quantum, to approximate the multimarginal optimal transport (MOT) distance between multiple discrete probability distributions.
main_result: The authors present a classical algorithm with a specific polynomial runtime bound and two distinct quantum algorithms—a projected subgradient method and a Sinkhorn variant—that achieve dimension speedups over classical counterparts.
method: The work uses techniques from convex optimization, formulating MOT as a linear program (LP) or its dual. Quantum approaches leverage quantum subroutines to accelerate the iterative solving of these LPs.
model_or_system: The model is purely mathematical/algorithmic: approximating the distance between $m$ discrete probability distributions ($\mu_1, \dots, \mu_m$), each supported on at most $n$ points. The problem structure generalizes classical Optimal Transport (OT).
key_observables: The primary observable is the MOT distance itself, approximated within an additive error $\varepsilon$. Other key quantities include the coupling tensor $X$ and its expected transportation cost.
important_parameters: Key parameters are $m$ (number of marginals), $n$ (support size), and $\varepsilon$ (desired accuracy). The complexity analysis depends heavily on these values.
main_assumptions: The quantum algorithms estimate the cost rather than returning an explicit coupling tensor, except in the case of the Sinkhorn algorithm which returns an implicit description. The classical bounds are derived for general MOT problems.
figures_summary: No specific figure summaries were extracted; the notes focus on algorithmic complexity and theoretical results presented across different methods (Primal/Dual LPs).
paper_structure: The paper is structured around formulating the MOT problem as an LP, presenting classical solutions for the primal form, and then detailing two distinct quantum algorithms—one based on projected subgradients applied to the dual, and another using a quantum Sinkhorn method for entropy regularization.
why_interesting: While not directly about physical Hamiltonians, the development of quantum algorithms for solving complex optimization problems like MOT is highly relevant. Quantum speedups in linear programming solvers are a major area of theoretical interest that could impact simulations in physics (e.g., calculating free energy differences or correlation functions via optimal transport metrics).
